package_info.package_name: a-function (and 85+ others, e.g., rush-lib, freezing, an-object, etc.)
package_info.why_malicious: These packages are part of a large-scale dependency confusion attack campaign. They are named after popular NodeJS/JavaScript functions and libraries to trick developers into installing them. All packages contain identical malicious code that fingerprints the host system and exfiltrates basic system information to an attacker-controlled server. The code includes logic to avoid execution on certain hostnames/usernames, likely to prevent accidental execution on the attacker's own systems.

execution_context.file_location: index.js (main entry point of each package)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, the code collects the system's hostname, username, and current working directory, then sends this data via HTTPS POST to 425a2.rt11.ml, enabling system fingerprinting and exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code exfiltrates host fingerprinting data to an external server without user consent, which is a classic indicator of malicious intent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal npm packages do not collect or transmit system information at import-time, especially not to untrusted third-party servers.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate telemetry or crash reporting tools may collect system data, but only with user consent and clear documentation.
key_indicators: Network exfiltration of host data at import-time
Targeting of sensitive fields (hostname, username, cwd)
Obfuscated or generic package names mimicking popular libraries

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, the code checks if the current system matches a list of hardcoded hostnames, usernames, or paths, and aborts execution if a match is found, acting as a kill switch.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The presence of kill switches to avoid execution on specific systems is a common anti-analysis and anti-researcher tactic in malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not contain logic to avoid running on specific hostnames or usernames.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Rarely, some software may avoid running in certain environments for licensing or compatibility reasons, but not in this context.
key_indicators: Hardcoded hostnames/usernames in kill switch logic

attack_chain.action: User installs or imports the malicious npm package, believing it to be a legitimate utility.
Malicious code checks if the current system matches any kill switch conditions (e.g., specific hostnames/usernames/paths).
attack_chain.leads_to: If a match is found, execution stops; otherwise, data collection proceeds.

attack_chain.action: System fingerprinting data (hostname, username, cwd) is collected.
Collected data is exfiltrated via HTTPS POST to the attacker's server (425a2.rt11.ml).

behavioral_signatures: Import-time execution of code that collects and exfiltrates system information
Presence of kill switch logic targeting specific hostnames/usernames/paths
Network requests to suspicious or newly registered domains during package import
file_indicators: index.js containing isValid function with hardcoded hostnames/usernames
Packages with version 99.X.X and empty or generic README files
network_indicators: Connections to domains not associated with the npm package's purported functionality
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for npm packages that execute code at import-time, especially those that collect and transmit system information externally. Flag packages with kill switch logic targeting specific hostnames/usernames. Alert on network connections to known malicious domains (e.g., 425a2.rt11.ml) originating from development or CI environments. Review packages with suspicious versioning (e.g., 99.X.X) and generic or misleading names.
